title: How Else Marie Pade, a Prisoner in World War II, Became Denmark’s First Female Electronic Composer

in History, Music, Uncategorized |   	September 25th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Before she became a com­pos­er of elec­tron­ic music, Else Marie Pade was a sick child lis­ten­ing to the radio. Fre­quent kid­ney inflam­ma­tions con­signed her to bed for long peri­ods of time, which would con­sti­tute nei­ther her last nor her harsh­est expe­ri­ence of con­fine­ment. She was still young when the Nazis occu­pied her home­land of Den­mark dur­ing World War II, and per­haps her youth explains her deci­sion to spit on a col­umn of march­ing Ger­man sol­diers. She escaped cap­ture that day, run­ning right into the Dan­ish Resis­tance, for which she dis­trib­uted under­ground news­pa­pers and trained in the use of explo­sives to cut off the ene­my’s tele­phone lines in the event of an Allied inva­sion. Arrest­ed by the Gestapo in 1944, she nev­er did get to exe­cute that plan, but her real ambi­tions turned out to be much larg­er.
“I screamed out loud in fear and help­less­ness in my soli­tary cell — but no one came,” Pade wrote in an essay pub­lished in The Wire. “It was then I promised myself that if I sur­vived this I would work with music for the rest of my life. And then I felt a strange calm: light, warmth and love were all around me. I was no longer alone. This was the turn­ing point in my life.” The very next day, “I start­ed scratch­ing staves on the prison wall with my garter belt fas­ten­er, and wrote out the theme that had come to me, inspired by the vision of the night.” Though infu­ri­at­ed at first, the Com­man­dant in charge told her he would “make sure that the Red Cross brought me music paper and writ­ing uten­sils so I would refrain from vio­lence and would not dirty the wall any more.”
Pade did all she could to com­pose dur­ing her time as a pris­on­er of war. After her trans­fer to the Frøslevle­jren intern­ment camp, she was reunit­ed with her piano teacher Karen Brieg, who’d brought her into the Resis­tance in the first place. “Karen wrote out Dan­ish songs for a three-part women’s choir, and I wrote schlagers — with which I want­ed to earn mon­ey for music stud­ies when we were released.” Her com­pa­tri­ots in the wom­en’s bar­racks promised to give her the oppor­tu­ni­ty to study at the Roy­al Dan­ish Acad­e­my of Music after the war’s end, which is exact­ly what she did. Though she entered the school with thoughts of becom­ing a pianist, a 1952 Dan­marks Radio broad­cast on Pierre Scha­ef­fer­’s musique con­crète per­ma­nent­ly changed the course of her artis­tic life.
Those sound col­lages turned musi­cal expe­ri­ences sent Pade back to her bouts of child­hood sick­ness, dur­ing which her chief plea­sures came from lis­ten­ing to the world around her. The result of this inspi­ra­tion was the first work of elec­tron­ic musique con­crète com­posed in Den­mark, A Day at Dyre­havs­bakken. Learn­ing from Scha­ef­fer, and lat­er from oth­er elec­tron­ic-music pio­neers like Karl­heinz Stock­hausen, Györ­gy Ligeti and Pierre Boulez, Pade devel­oped the abil­i­ty to real­ize the musi­cal worlds she’s been explor­ing in her head all along. Their aus­tere sound­scapes could hard­ly be far­ther from the sen­ti­men­tal schlager bal­lads she’d writ­ten to keep spir­its up in the bar­racks, but as you can hear in the selec­tion from 1985 to 1995 pre­sent­ed in the com­pi­la­tion above, the son­ic imag­i­na­tion that heard an ambi­ent sym­pho­ny in drip­ping sponges, whistling ket­tles, singing birds, and trot­ting hors­es remains exhil­a­rat­ing today.
Relat­ed con­tent:
Hear Sev­en Hours of Women Mak­ing Elec­tron­ic Music (1938–2014)
Daphne Oram Cre­at­ed the BBC’s First-Ever Piece of Elec­tron­ic Music (1957)
The Fas­ci­nat­ing Sto­ry of How the Elec­tric Music Pio­neer Delia Der­byshire Cre­at­ed the Orig­i­nal Doc­tor Who Theme (1963)
What is Elec­tron­ic Music?: Pio­neer­ing Elec­tron­ic Musi­cian Daphne Oram Explains (1969)
New Doc­u­men­tary Sis­ters with Tran­sis­tors Tells the Sto­ry of Elec­tron­ic Music’s Female Pio­neers
Hear Elec­tron­ic Lady­land, a Mix­tape Fea­tur­ing 55 Tracks from 35 Pio­neer­ing Women in Elec­tron­ic Music
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Three Artists and Two Writers On Surrealist Painter Remedios Varo's Influence
description: Like the Argentinian writer Samanta Schweblin, the first time I found myself in front of a painting by the Spanish-Mexican artist Remedios Varo (1
body:
Like the Argentinian writer Samanta Schweblin, the first time I found myself in front of a painting by the Spanish-Mexican artist Remedios Varo (1908-1963), I was stunned. Who was this elegant owl-figure with dainty fingers and feet? What was animating the creaturely machine at her side with tentacle-like brushes as hands? And, would I ever be able to look away?
Feeling mesmerized and awe-struck by Varo’s Surrealist visions isn’t an uncommon position to find oneself in. A new release from Louisiana Channel interviews three artists and two writers—Schweblin being one—about Varo’s influence, particularly her precise approach to alchemy and visualizing the thin veil between the physical and spiritual world. Interspersing artworks and commentary creates an insightful tapestry of a singular artist and her enduring legacy. Watch “Remedios Varo: The Painter of Magic” below, and learn more about the artist previously on Colossal.

title: Fantastic Plants Spring from Taehyoung Maria Jeon's Digital Illustrations
description: “I try to avoid playing it safe or going for the obvious. Instead, I look at plants from a different perspective and express them in my own way,”
body:
“I try to avoid playing it safe or going for the obvious. Instead, I look at plants from a different perspective and express them in my own way,” South Korean artist Taehyoung Maria Jeon says about a fantastical series of illustrations. “Ironically, having rules is what gives me the freedom to experiment with plant shape.”
Although she’s trained as a printmaker and continues to build compositions in layers, Jeon turns to digital methods as she reimagines the specimens cohabitating in her apartment, beginning with leaves and stems before venturing into surreal terrain. Purple veins, red outlines, and a smattering of stars appear on the imagined life forms, their vivid color palettes furthering their sense of the uncanny.

Titled Plant Series, the project “started as a personal challenge to fill a square canvas with plants, playing with shapes and composition to pack everything in as much as possible,” she says. “As the series continues, the drawings evolve and the nuances shift, but at its heart, it is always about composition, balance, colour, and shape—and hopefully sending out positive vibes, too.”
Dozens of illustrations from the series are compiled in Folium, Jeon’s first monograph from Volume. The publisher functions like Kickstarter and asks readers to back the project before printing. You can reserve your copy on Volume’s website, and find more from the artist on Instagram.

title: On Concrete Remnants of London's Aylesbury Estate, Harriet Mena Hill Preserves a Community
description: Built throughout the 1960s and ’70s, the Aylesbury Estate is an enormous public housing complex in South East London that at its peak, boasted 11,
body:
Built throughout the 1960s and ’70s, the Aylesbury Estate is an enormous public housing complex in South East London that at its peak, boasted 11,000 residents. Like other social projects of this kind, Aylesbury has struggled with violence and vandalism throughout its run, and in 2005, local officials decided to demolish the estate and rebuild in phases rather than rehabilitate the existing structures.
Living and working in South East London for nearly four decades, Harriet Mena Hill was familiar with the area, but it wasn’t until 2018 when she was commissioned to teach a summer program for young residents that she really engaged with the project. She made large portraits from wool, blending dyed roving to delineate windows, shape bowed electrical wires, and even mimic graffiti spray-painted on outdoor walls. 
“Soft Concrete Missenden, Aylesbury Estate” (2020), wool on felt, 88 x 118 centimeters
Forming the series Soft Concrete, the textile pieces cast a largely gray environment of stone and steel in soft fiber. The body of work, Hill says, was a “repositioning of how the estate is perceived. Historically, it has been widely portrayed in the media as violent and intimidating, as a place without hope.” 
In contrast, Soft Concrete “presents the estate as a place of living and community. From a distance, the portraits look like photographs or realistic paintings, but on closer inspection, the material reveals itself to be wool, hand blended for subtle colour mixing used to depict small active details of domestic life,” the artist adds.
Hill is broadly interested in the ways that communities and the objects they interact with can become vessels for shared memories, so when the estate began to be razed in 2020, she started to collect fragments of concrete from the construction site. “It was a direct response to the situation of residents who were required to stay at home as the demolition of adjoining blocks, the homes of their former neighbours, continued throughout lockdown, in spite of wider restrictions,” she tells Colossal.
Before its destruction, several tenants had advocated for renovations rather than demolition, hoping to preserve the community and homes they’d built. In an interview with the BBC in 2023, long-time resident Aysen Dennis lamented being forced to leave the estate after 30 years. Local administrators found her new housing in central London, but it wasn’t the same. “The council gave me everything I asked for. It’s on a high floor. There’s lots of light. I can see the park,” Dennis said. “But it’s not my home.”
Studio view. Photo by Jon Cardwell
Intimate in scale, Hill’s paintings glimpse hallways and pockets of windows that are similarly sliced from their larger contexts, the ragged edges of concrete framing the largely domestic spaces. Part of the ongoing series titled The Aylesbury Fragments, the scenes capture the run-down infrastructure of buildings left standing during the phased reconstruction process. 
Although regeneration began in 2013, it’s less than half complete, and Hill has completed more than 150 paintings to date. As demolition continues, she adds to her ever-changing collection of concrete remnants. “I live with the unpainted pieces for months, sometimes years, getting to know their shape before I begin working on them,” the artist says, noting that as long as there are buildings still under construction, she’ll continue painting these small tributes to the community once housed within their walls.
Hill has exhibitions slated for London and across the U.K. throughout 2027. Follow along on Instagram.

title: El Museo del Barrio Apologizes for Renting Space for 9/11 Conspiracy Event
description:
News
                The Harlem institution said it was "not aware of the full program, content and speaker list for this event.
body:
News
                The Harlem institution said it was "not aware of the full program, content and speaker list for this event.”  
            
                
                                
                            
                
                
                    Anna Lee
                    September 24, 2026
                            — 2 min read
                    
                
            
                
        
            The theater at the El Museo del Barrio in East Harlem (photo Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
    
        
            The El Museo del Barrio in New York has expressed regret at providing rental space for a conspiracy-filled conference on the 25th anniversary of 9/11, as first reported by the New York Times.The East Harlem museum, which houses a trove of artworks by artists of Latin American descent, rented out part of its building to the International Center for 9/11 Justice for “Turning the Tide: 9/11 25 Years Later." The conference ran from September 10 through September 13, with first responders, elected officials, and victims' family members, among others, participating. Speakers included Bill Manning, the former chief editor-in-chief of Fire Engineering magazine, who theorized that the buildings fell from controlled demolition, and retired Lieutenant Colonel Karen Kwiatkowski, who said the federal government covered up events including 9/11 and podcaster Charlie Kirk's assassination. Roger Waters of the band Pink Floyd also spoke, expressing his desire to probe “what actually happened” on 9/11.  "El Museo del Barrio recognizes its responsibility as a steward of the public trust and deeply regrets this event,” the museum said in a statement shared with Hyperallergic. “At the time of contracting, the Museum was not aware of the full program, content and speaker list for this event.”

title: No One Is Reading, Except at the New York Art Book Fair
description:
Feature
                The overlooked, subversive, and playful currents of politics and queer culture flow freely at the fair’s
body:
Feature
                The overlooked, subversive, and playful currents of politics and queer culture flow freely at the fair’s 20th anniversary edition, held at MoMA PS1. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Ruiqi Ma and Nathan Nam of com,,,as at the Printed Matter art book fair (all photos Lakshmi Rivera Amin/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            If Reading Rainbow’s opening sequence — the Y2K-techno-optimistic Chaka Khan version, to be exact — were a real place, it would be the outdoor zine tent at the New York Art Book Fair. I delight in never quite knowing what to expect from the annual gathering organized by Printed Matter, and this year was no different: Over 300 exhibitors from across the world come together at MoMA PS1 in Queens to form a giant, chimeric bookstore of sorts that feels unmistakably alive.On opening night of the fair’s 20th anniversary edition, which runs through the weekend, staffers handed us plastic string-closure folders, complete with lenticular Tweety Bird prints, for storing the many zines, flyers, and uncategorizable artworks we’d encounter inside. Across from artist Precious Okoyomon’s sculpture in the courtyard, the zine tent felt like a pocket-sized universe where marginalia is the text, and the overlooked, subversive, and playful currents of politics and queer culture flow freely.Staffers outside the fair handed us plastic string-closure folders to hold the treasures we'd encounter inside.Exhibit A: Art workers Jenna Hamed, Aya Krisht, and Rhonda Khalifeh of the Book Arts Solidarity Network handed out flyers for a publishers' meet-up after the fair, a space for connection beyond the museum’s walls. The organization first formed as a way to challenge book institutions’ silence on the genocide in Palestine, and is now launching its third annual edition of the MAKEREADY publication. For the risograph-printed booklet, they collected paintings, photographs, and written reflections from four artists in Gaza and South Lebanon, soon realizing that one thread connected all the works: the color yellow. Hamed explained that the process of assembling the poetic publication was “cathartic,” a way to process an era of bald imperialism and dispossession by centering the artists who are witnessing it.“It really came out of skill,” Hamed said of the organization’s ability to collaborate across borders. “We know what we’re doing.”

title: Lisa Bradley Moves Beyond Luminosity at the Delaware Art Museum
description:
Announcement
                The Delaware Art Museum presents the artist’s newest body of work in a solo exhibition spanning recent l
body:
Announcement
                The Delaware Art Museum presents the artist’s newest body of work in a solo exhibition spanning recent large-scale paintings and early works on paper.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Omnipresent, 2018, Lisa Bradley (born 1951), Oil on canvas, 74 1/2 × 55 in. (189.2 × 139.7 cm), Courtesy of the artist., © Lisa BradleyThe Delaware Art Museum is proud to present Lisa Bradley: Beyond Luminosity, opening September 19, 2026. Beyond Luminosity offers a new opportunity to engage with Bradley’s most recent body of work, presented publicly for the first time. The exhibition is organized by DelArt Head Curator and Curator of Contemporary Art Margaret Winslow and Art Bridges Fellow Hilda Delgado.“We are rewarded with each encounter, suspended in a luminous field of color,” says Winslow, reflecting on Bradley’s work.Bradley translates the mysterious into the physical with intimate marks and sweeping gestures. As an artist working within the field of abstraction, Bradley has contributed to its evolving history. Art historian Carter Ratcliff describes her work as depicting “a pause between the pulses of some vast and luminous energy.” The artist’s career is one that has endured beyond trends and common tropes, representing a breakthrough in the field of abstract painting. Bradley’s work is informed by a strong interest in spiritual experience. In her luminous paintings, she achieves an expression of simultaneous movement and stillness, creating a feeling of suspended time.DelArt invites audiences to experience new work by contemporary artists through exhibitions that offer fresh perspectives and deepen connections to the Museum’s collection. Lisa Bradley: Beyond Luminosity builds on this commitment, presenting 10 large-scale paintings and eight works on paper in DelArt’s solo exhibition of Bradley’s work. The presentation also extends the Museum’s longstanding connection to the artist. Bradley’s Akasa II entered DelArt’s collection in 2009 and, over the past 15 years, has been a regular presence in the galleries, captivating visitors of all ages and becoming a beloved piece in the contemporary collection.A complementary 120-page monograph features insights from prominent curators, critics, and art historians.Learn more at delart.org.
